topics.title: Discriminated Union — what and where?
topics.html:
Union where each branch shares a literal-typed field (discriminant). TS automatically narrows after checking. Makes invalid states physically impossible.

type AsyncState<T> =
  | { status: "idle" }
  | { status: "loading" }
  | { status: "success"; data: T }
  | { status: "error"; error: string };

function DataView({ state }: { state: AsyncState<User> }) {
  switch (state.status) {
    case "loading": return <Spinner />;
    case "error": return <ErrorMsg msg={state.error} />;
    case "success": return <UserCard user={state.data} />;
    default: { const _: never = state; return null; } // exhaustive check
  }
}
💬 Say it like this

Instead of having isLoading, data, and error as three separate values that can all be set at once, you model it as a union with a status field. TypeScript then knows exactly what fields are available in each branch — no runtime checks needed.

The never at the end is a compile-time exhaustiveness check. Add a new status to the union and forget to handle it in the switch — TypeScript throws an error at build time.

topics.title: Mapped types and conditional types.
topics.html:
// Mapped types — transform each key of a type
type Nullable<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] | null };
type FormErrors<T> = Partial<Record<keyof T, string>>;
// Conditional types — if/else at type level
type AwaitedT<T> = T extends Promise<infer U> ? AwaitedT<U> : T;
type ReturnTypeOf<T> = T extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never;
// DeepPartial
type DeepPartial<T> = T extends object ? { [P in keyof T]?: DeepPartial<T[P]> } : T;
// satisfies (TS 4.9+) — validate without widening
const palette = { red: "#ff0000" } satisfies Record<string, string>;
palette.red; // type is "#ff0000" (literal), not string
// Implement Pick yourself (common interview question):
type MyPick<T, K extends keyof T> = { [P in K]: T[P] };
💬 Say it like this

A mapped type walks over the keys of another type and transforms them — that is how Partial and Readonly are built. A conditional type is an if-else at the type level, and infer lets me pull a type out of another one, like the return type of a function.

I use them to keep one source of truth. For example, form error types are generated from the form data type, so when a field is added, the error type updates by itself.

topics.title: Most-used utility types.
topics.html:
Partial<T>       // all props optional
Required<T>      // all props required
Readonly<T>      // all props readonly
Pick<T, K>       // keep only keys K
Omit<T, K>       // drop keys K
Record<K, V>     // { [k in K]: V }
ReturnType<F>    // return type of function F
Parameters<F>   // tuple of parameter types
Awaited<T>       // unwrap Promise<T>
NonNullable<T>   // exclude null/undefined
💬 Say it like this

These are the ones I use every day: Partial and Required for optional fields, Pick and Omit to build a smaller type from a bigger one, Record for dictionaries, and ReturnType or Awaited to derive types from functions and promises.

The point is always the same: derive types from what already exists instead of writing the same shape twice.

topics.title: Generic constraints — extends, keyof, default types.
topics.html:
• T extends X — constrains T to be assignable to X. Without constraints, T is basically any.
  • K extends keyof T — K must be a key of T. Return type narrows to T[K] automatically.
  • Default type params: T = string — lets callers omit the type argument.
  • Multiple constraints via intersection: T extends A & B (no extends A, B syntax).
// Constrained generic — return type is T[K], not any
function getProperty<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] {
  return obj[key];
}

// Multiple constraints via intersection
function merge<T extends object, U extends object>(a: T, b: U): T & U {
  return { ...a, ...b };
}

// Default type param — ApiResponse without T argument is valid
type ApiResponse<T = unknown> = { data: T; status: number };

// Classic interview: type-safe pluck
function pluck<T, K extends keyof T>(arr: T[], key: K): T[K][] {
  return arr.map(item => item[key]);
}
pluck([{ name: "Alice", age: 30 }], "name"); // string[]
pluck([{ name: "Alice", age: 30 }], "age");  // number[]

// Constructor constraint — accept a class, return an instance
function create<T>(Ctor: new (...args: any[]) => T): T {
  return new Ctor();
}
💬 Say it like this

Generics without constraints let you write flexible code but you can't actually do anything with the value inside — TS treats it as opaque. T extends keyof U is the key pattern: it locks T to only valid property names of U, so the return type narrows to U[T] automatically. That's how pluck knows it returns string[] or number[] depending on the key you pass in. Default type params remove boilerplate for the 90% case — like making ApiResponse work without specifying T when you don't care about the data shape yet.

T extends object vs T extends {}?
T extends {} includes everything except null/undefined — practically the same as unknown. T extends object excludes primitives (string, number, boolean). For plain objects use T extends Record<string, unknown>.
Why does new T() fail inside a generic function?
TS doesn't know T has a constructor. Fix: pass the constructor explicitly as Ctor: new (...args: any[]) => T. ConstructorParameters<typeof Ctor> gets its param types.

topics.title: Type guards — narrowing, is predicates, assertion functions.
topics.html:
• Built-in narrowing: typeof, instanceof, in operator, truthiness checks.
  • Custom type predicates: return type value is T — tells TS "if this returns true, narrow to T".
  • Assertion functions: return type asserts value is T — throws on failure, narrows everything after the call.
// typeof + instanceof
function format(val: string | number) {
  if (typeof val === "string") return val.toUpperCase(); // string
  return val.toFixed(2); // number
}

// in operator narrowing
type A = { x: number };
type B = { y: string };
function handle(v: A | B) {
  if ("x" in v) v.x; // A
  else v.y;          // B
}

// Custom type predicate — "trust me, if true it's a Dog"
interface Cat { meow(): void; }
interface Dog { bark(): void; }
function isDog(pet: Cat | Dog): pet is Dog {
  return "bark" in pet;
}

// Assertion function — throws if not string, narrows after call
function assertIsString(val: unknown): asserts val is string {
  if (typeof val !== "string") throw new Error(`Expected string, got ${typeof val}`);
}
function process(val: unknown) {
  assertIsString(val);
  val.toUpperCase(); // string — TS knows
}

// Array filter with inline type guard (very common in practice)
const items: (string | null)[] = ["a", null, "b"];
const strings = items.filter((x): x is string => x !== null);
// type: string[]  (without the guard it would stay (string | null)[])
💬 Say it like this

Type guards are how TypeScript knows which branch of a union you're in. Built-in ones — typeof, instanceof, in — work automatically. When you have custom logic, you return pet is Dog instead of boolean. That return type is a contract: "when I return true, trust me it's a Dog." The difference between a predicate and an assertion function: predicate narrows only inside the if branch; assertion function throws on failure and narrows everything that comes after, unconditionally. The inline filter pattern is one I use constantly — without it, .filter(x => x !== null) still gives you (string | null)[].

Predicate vs assertion function?
Predicate returns boolean — narrowing only in the if-true branch. Assertion function returns void and throws — narrowing applies to all code after the call.

topics.title: infer keyword — extract parts of complex types.
topics.html:
• infer only works inside extends clauses of conditional types.
  • TS pattern-matches the shape and binds whatever it finds to the infer variable.
  • Multiple infer bindings in one conditional is valid.
// Implement ReturnType from scratch (classic interview)
type MyReturnType<T> = T extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never;

// Awaited — unwrap any depth of Promise
type MyAwaited<T> = T extends Promise<infer U> ? MyAwaited<U> : T;
type X = MyAwaited<Promise<Promise<string>>>; // string

// Extract array element type
type ArrayItem<T> = T extends (infer U)[] ? U : never;
type S = ArrayItem<string[]>; // string

// Extract head and last from tuple (rest patterns)
type Head<T extends any[]> = T extends [infer H, ...any[]] ? H : never;
type Last<T extends any[]> = T extends [...any[], infer L] ? L : never;
type H = Head<[number, string, boolean]>; // number
type L = Last<[number, string, boolean]>;  // boolean

// Multiple infer bindings — extract first param and return type together
type FirstArgAndReturn<T> = T extends (first: infer F, ...rest: any[]) => infer R
  ? { arg: F; ret: R }
  : never;
type Info = FirstArgAndReturn<(x: number, y: string) => boolean>;
// { arg: number; ret: boolean }

// Real use case: unwrap async thunk return
type UnwrapThunk<T> = T extends () => Promise<infer U> ? U : never;
💬 Say it like this

infer is a placeholder you put inside a conditional type's extends clause. TypeScript pattern-matches the shape and binds whatever it finds there to that name. The canonical example is implementing ReturnType: you're saying "if T looks like a function returning something, bind that something to R, and that's your result." Without infer, you can only check assignability — you can't extract parts. The tuple rest pattern with [infer H, ...any[]] is especially useful for type-level list manipulation.

Can infer be used outside a conditional type?
No — syntax error. Only valid inside the extends clause of a conditional type.
What if the infer pattern doesn't match?
The false branch is taken and you get never (in the typical pattern). T extends (...args) => infer R ? R : never → if T is not a function, result is never.

topics.title: Template literal types — string manipulation at the type level.
topics.html:
// Combine unions into string combinations
type Dir = "top" | "right" | "bottom" | "left";
type CSSProp = `margin-${Dir}` | `padding-${Dir}`;
// = "margin-top" | "margin-right" | ... | "padding-left"

// Event handler name generation
type EventName = "click" | "focus" | "blur";
type HandlerName = `on${Capitalize<EventName>}`;
// = "onClick" | "onFocus" | "onBlur"

// Intrinsic string utilities
type U = Uppercase<"hello">;    // "HELLO"
type L = Lowercase<"WORLD">;    // "world"
type C = Capitalize<"hello">;   // "Hello"
type N = Uncapitalize<"Hello">; // "hello"

// Derive setter names from state shape
type Setters<T> = {
  [K in keyof T as `set${Capitalize<K & string>}`]: (val: T[K]) => void
};
type CounterSetters = Setters<{ count: number; label: string }>;
// { setCount: (val: number) => void; setLabel: (val: string) => void }

// Type-safe dot-notation paths (i18n / config)
type Paths<T> = T extends object ? {
  [K in keyof T]: K extends string
    ? T[K] extends object ? `${K}.${Paths<T[K]>}` : K
    : never
}[keyof T] : never;
type UserPaths = Paths<{ user: { name: string; age: number } }>;
// "user.name" | "user.age"
💬 Say it like this

Template literal types bring the same backtick syntax you use in JavaScript to the type level. When you use a union inside the template, TypeScript expands it into every combination — so `margin-${Dir}` automatically generates all four directions. The Capitalize family of intrinsic utilities handles case transformations. Combined with mapped type key remapping using as, you can automatically derive entire interfaces — the setter-generation pattern is a real one I've used in Zustand stores to avoid writing setters by hand.

topics.title: Branded / Nominal types — prevent structural type confusion.
topics.html:
TypeScript uses structural typing: two identical shapes are always assignable to each other. Branded types add a phantom property to make primitives type-distinct at compile time with zero runtime cost.

// Problem: both UserId and OrderId are just string — TS allows swapping
function sendEmail(userId: string, orderId: string) {}
// sendEmail(orderId, userId) compiles — silent bug

// Solution: unique symbol brand
declare const __brand: unique symbol;
type Brand<T, B> = T & { readonly [__brand]: B };

type UserId  = Brand<string, "UserId">;
type OrderId = Brand<string, "OrderId">;

// Constructor functions — the only place you cast
const toUserId  = (id: string): UserId  => id as UserId;
const toOrderId = (id: string): OrderId => id as OrderId;

const uid = toUserId("u_123");
const oid = toOrderId("o_456");
sendEmail(uid, oid); // ✓
sendEmail(oid, uid); // ✗ Error: OrderId not assignable to UserId

// Common use cases: units of measure
type Milliseconds = Brand<number, "Milliseconds">;
type Seconds      = Brand<number, "Seconds">;
// Can't accidentally pass milliseconds where seconds expected

type Pixels = Brand<number, "Pixels">;
type Rem    = Brand<number, "Rem">;

// Branded string for validated data
type Email     = Brand<string, "Email">;
type SafeHtml  = Brand<string, "SafeHtml">;
function sanitize(html: string): SafeHtml { return DOMPurify.sanitize(html) as SafeHtml; }
function render(html: SafeHtml) { el.innerHTML = html; } // only accepts sanitized
💬 Say it like this

TypeScript's structural typing means any two string values are always interchangeable — which is fine until you have UserId and OrderId that happen to both be strings but should never be swapped. Branded types attach a phantom property using a unique symbol as the key — it only exists at the type level, zero runtime overhead. You cast once inside a constructor function, and everywhere else TypeScript enforces the distinction. The pattern scales well to units of measure, validated types like SafeHtml, or database ID columns that shouldn't be mixed.

topics.title: as const and satisfies — freeze literals and validate without widening.
topics.html:
// as const — keep literal types, make readonly
const ROUTES = {
  home: "/",
  profile: "/profile",
  settings: "/settings",
} as const;
// Without: { home: string; profile: string; ... }
// With:    { readonly home: "/"; readonly profile: "/profile"; ... }

// Extract union from as const object
type Route = typeof ROUTES[keyof typeof ROUTES]; // "/" | "/profile" | "/settings"

// as const array → readonly tuple with literal types
const SIZES = ["sm", "md", "lg"] as const;
type Size = typeof SIZES[number]; // "sm" | "md" | "lg"

// Enum alternative — no emitted JS, works with JSON, tree-shakeable
const STATUS = ["idle", "loading", "success", "error"] as const;
type Status = typeof STATUS[number];

// satisfies (TS 4.9+) — validate shape AND keep literal inference
const palette1: Record<string, string> = { red: "#ff0000" };
palette1.red; // type: string — literal lost

const palette2 = { red: "#ff0000", green: "#00ff00" } satisfies Record<string, string>;
palette2.red; // type: "#ff0000" — literal preserved AND validated

// Combine: freeze + validate
const config = {
  endpoint: "https://api.example.com",
  timeout: 5000,
} as const satisfies { endpoint: string; timeout: number };
💬 Say it like this

as const tells TypeScript: don't widen these literals, keep the exact values. Without it, "/profile" becomes string. With it, you can extract a union of all exact values. This is the modern alternative to enums — as const array plus typeof arr[number] for the union type. No emitted code, JSON-serializable, tree-shakeable.

satisfies solves a different problem. A type annotation widens your literals to match the annotation type. satisfies validates the shape without widening — you get both the type check AND the literal types preserved for dot-access. Combining both gives you type safety at its best.

topics.title: Function overloads — correlated input/output types.
topics.html:
// Problem: union return type loses the input-output relationship
function parse(input: string | number): string | number { return input; }
parse("hello"); // type: string | number — imprecise

// Solution: overload signatures (these are the public API)
function parse(input: string): string;
function parse(input: number): number;
function parse(input: string | number): string | number { // implementation — not visible to callers
  return typeof input === "string" ? input.trim() : Math.round(input);
}
parse("hello"); // string ✓
parse(42);      // number ✓

// Tag-based overloads — createElement style
function createElement(tag: "a"): HTMLAnchorElement;
function createElement(tag: "div"): HTMLDivElement;
function createElement(tag: string): HTMLElement;
function createElement(tag: string): HTMLElement {
  return document.createElement(tag);
}

// Class method overloads
class EventEmitter {
  on(event: "data", listener: (data: Buffer) => void): this;
  on(event: "error", listener: (err: Error) => void): this;
  on(event: string, listener: (...args: any[]) => void): this {
    // implementation
    return this;
  }
}
💬 Say it like this

Overloads let you express that the return type depends on the specific input type — something a union return type can't capture. The rules: overload signatures are the public API, the implementation signature is private and must be compatible with all of them. TypeScript checks calls against overload signatures in order, top to bottom, so put the most specific ones first. I reach for overloads when I need correlated input-output types — like a function that returns different shapes based on a discriminant tag. For simple optional params, optional params or a union are usually cleaner.

topics.title: Declaration merging & module augmentation — extend types you don't own.
topics.html:
// Augment a third-party module (most common real-world use)
// File: types/express.d.ts
import "express";
declare module "express-serve-static-core" {
  interface Request {
    user?: { id: string; role: "admin" | "user" };
  }
}
// req.user is now typed everywhere without casting

// Augment React Navigation type-safe param list
// File: types/navigation.d.ts
declare global {
  namespace ReactNavigation {
    interface RootParamList extends RootStackParamList {}
  }
}

// Module declaration for non-TS files
// File: types/assets.d.ts
declare module "*.svg" {
  const content: React.FunctionComponent<React.SVGAttributes<SVGElement>>;
  export default content;
}
declare module "*.png" {
  const src: string;
  export default src;
}

// Interface merging — open interfaces can be extended anywhere (unlike type aliases)
interface Window {
  analytics: AnalyticsClient;
}
// Works because interfaces are "open" — type aliases are "closed"

// Global augmentation
declare global {
  interface Array<T> {
    last(): T | undefined;
  }
}
💬 Say it like this

Module augmentation is how you add types to libraries you don't own. The classic cases: adding a user field to Express's Request, extending React Navigation's param list for type-safe navigation, or typing SVG imports so you can import them as React components. You create a .d.ts file, import the target module, and use declare module. TypeScript merges your declaration with the original. Interface merging works because interfaces are "open" — you can add to them from anywhere. Type aliases are closed — you can't do this with type.

interface vs type — when to pick which?
Interface: use for object shapes, class contracts, public APIs, anything that needs declaration merging. Type alias: unions, intersections, mapped types, conditional types, template literal types, tuples — everything interface can't express. Practical rule: interface for objects, type for everything else.

topics.title: keyof, typeof, and lookup types — the core trio.
topics.html:
const user = { id: 1, name: "Alice", role: "admin" as const };

// typeof — infer type from a value (variable → type)
type User = typeof user;
// { id: number; name: string; role: "admin" }

// keyof — union of all property names
type UserKey = keyof User; // "id" | "name" | "role"
type UserKey2 = keyof typeof user; // same — combine typeof + keyof (very common)

// Lookup type T[K] — extract the type of a property
type UserName = User["name"]; // string
type UserRole = User["role"]; // "admin"

// Index with a union to get union of value types
type UserValues = User[keyof User]; // number | string | "admin"

// keyof on union type — only shared keys
type AB = { a: string } | { b: number };
type Keys = keyof AB; // never (no shared keys)

// Array indexed access — extract element type
const routes = ["/", "/about", "/settings"] as const;
type Route = typeof routes[number]; // "/" | "/about" | "/settings"

// Practical: type-safe event handler map
type EventMap = { click: MouseEvent; focus: FocusEvent; keydown: KeyboardEvent };
function on<K extends keyof EventMap>(event: K, cb: (e: EventMap[K]) => void) {
  document.addEventListener(event, cb as EventListener);
}
on("click", (e) => e.clientX);  // MouseEvent — fully inferred, no cast needed
on("keydown", (e) => e.key);    // KeyboardEvent
💬 Say it like this

These three work together constantly. typeof extracts a type from a runtime value — great when you have a config object and want the type to automatically stay in sync with the value. keyof gives you a union of all property names — you use it to constrain generic parameters to valid keys. Lookup types index into a type the way you index into an object — T["name"] gives you the type of the name property. The combination keyof typeof someObject is everywhere in real code: it gives you the literal key union of a value without manually listing anything. The EventMap pattern is a personal favorite — a single generic function that narrows the callback parameter based on which event name you pass in.

topics.title: tsconfig strict flags — what actually matters.
topics.html:
FlagWhat it doesPriority
strictUmbrella: enables all flags belowAlways on
strictNullChecksnull/undefined not assignable to other typesMost impactful single flag
strictFunctionTypesFunction params checked contravariantlyPrevents covariant callback bugs
noImplicitAnyError on implicit anyForces explicit types everywhere
noUncheckedIndexedAccessarr[0] returns T | undefinedNot in strict — add manually
exactOptionalPropertyTypes{ x?: string } rejects { x: undefined }Optional ≠ undefined-valued
 
// strictNullChecks
function getName(user: User | null): string {
  return user.name;          // ✗ user might be null
  return user?.name ?? "–";  // ✓
}

// noUncheckedIndexedAccess — arr[0] is T | undefined, not T
const arr = [1, 2, 3];
const first = arr[0]; // number | undefined
if (first !== undefined) first.toFixed(); // safe

// exactOptionalPropertyTypes
interface Config { timeout?: number; }
const c: Config = { timeout: undefined }; // ✗ — optional ≠ explicitly undefined
// must either set a value or omit the key entirely

// Useful tsconfig extras beyond strict
// "moduleResolution": "bundler"  — for Vite / modern bundlers
// "verbatimModuleSyntax": true   — TS 5.0+: import type enforced where needed
// "isolatedModules": true        — safe for Babel / esbuild transpilation
💬 Say it like this

Always start with "strict": true — it's an umbrella that enables all the important checks. The most impactful individual flag is strictNullChecks: without it, null and undefined are silently assignable to everything, which hides an entire class of runtime errors. Two flags I always add beyond strict: noUncheckedIndexedAccess makes array indexing honest — arr[0] is T | undefined, not a lie that it's always T. And exactOptionalPropertyTypes makes optional properties mean "may not be present" rather than "may be undefined" — a subtle but important distinction.
